```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```


# Introduction

This document is dedicated to doing exploratory data analysis on the superstore dataset. In this dataset, each row corresponds with a purchase of an individual product made by a customer. For orders with multiple products purchased, each individual product has it's own row, but the order number remains the same for the entire order.

The selected variables in this dataset are described below:

| Variable     | Description                                 |              Type |
|-----------------------------|:-------------------|----------------------:|
| OrderID      | Order number for the entire purchase made.  |         Character |
| OrderDate    | Date on which the order was placed.         |              Date |
| ShipDate     | Date on which the order was shipped.        |              Date |
| ShipMode     | Method by which the order was shipped.      |            Factor |
| CustomerID   | ID Assigned to Customer.                    |         Character |
| CustomerName | Name of customer.                           |         Character |
| Segment      | Category of purchaser type/purpose.         |            Factor |
| City         | City in which the order was placed.         |            Factor |
| State        | State in which the order was placed.        |            Factor |
| PostalCode   | Postal code in which the order was placed.  |           Numeric |
| Region       | Region in which the order was placed.       |            Factor |
| ProductID    | ID assigned to the product.                 |         Character |
| Category     | Category of the product type.               |            Factor |
| Subcategory  | Subcategory of the product type.            |            Factor |
| ProductName  | Full name of the product.                   |         Character |
| Sales        | Selling price of the product.               |           Numeric |
| Quantity     | Number of quantity AVAILABLE of the product | Numeric (Integer) |
| Discount     | Discount available on each product          |           Numeric |
| Profit       | Profit gained on the product.               |           Numeric |

Note: The raw dataset includes 2 additional variables, RowID and Country, which are both redundant (RowID is just row number, Country is always US), and thus were removed.

For the sake of simplicity, the categorical variables I will be focusing on are Region, Segment, and Category, as they are of greatest interest to me.

# Contingency Tables

## One-Way Contingency Tables

I will create three one-way contingency tables. The first will count the number of products sold by consumer segment, the second will count by region, and the final will count by category of the product.

### Number of Products Sold by Segment (Consumer Category)

First, we will tally the number of purchases by the consumer type, known as the segment.

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Segment) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

The greatest number of purchases were made by average consumers, followed by corporate purchases, and finally home offices.

### Number of Products Sold by Region

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Region) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

The most products were sold in the West region, and the least were sold in the South region.

### Number of Products Sold by Product Category

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

The most common category of products sold was office supplies, while the least common category of products sold was in technology.

## Two-Way Contingency Tables

Next, we will look at the same variables from the data through three two-way contingency tables. The first table will look at number of products sold by segment and region, the second by region and category, and the third by category and segment.

### Number of Products Sold by Segment and Region

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Segment,Region) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Region, values_from = count)
```

It seems that most consumer purchases were made in the East, and the most corporate and home office purchases were made in the West. The South made the least purchases across all three categories.

### Number of Products Sold by Region and Category

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Region,Category) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Category, values_from = count)
```

The most of all three categories was purchased in the West, while the least was purchased in the South.

### Number of Products Sold by Category and Segment

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Category,Segment) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Segment, values_from = count)
```

Consumers purchase more of all three categories than corporate and home offices purchasers combined.

## Contingency Table Conclusion

It would seem that the greatest number of products sold are sold to consumers are consumers, sold in the West, and specifically office supplies. The greatest areas for growth are home offices purchasers, the Southern region, and technology products.

# Numerical Summaries

In order to gain a greater understanding of the numeric side of the data, we need to find basic numerical summaries for our numeric variables, which include Sales, Quantity, Discount, and Profit.

We will start by looking at these variables on the baseline level, and then will group them by our headline categorical variables to find more specific insights.

## General Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn} {.col}"))
```

Since Sales represents price, the average price of the products sold is \$229.86, which is much higher than our median price of \$54.49. This implies that most of what is sold is lower ticket items, while there are a few stand-out high ticket items which pull up the average.

The average quantity we have on hand is 3.78, which is greater than the median quantity on hand. This implies that most items are not stocked in larger numbers, but a few are stocked in higher quantities.

The average discount of around 15\% is lower than the median discount of 20\%. This is most likely because some items are not on discount at all, which drags the mean down, even if most items do have some discount.

The profit situation is similar to that of sales price, wil the mean profit of $28.66 being much higher than the median of \$8.67, most likely for the same reason.

## Specific Numerical Summaries

We will start with numerical summaries individually by region, segment, and category, and then we will cross of variables of interest for additionally summaries.

### Region Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Region) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```

Despite the number of products sold in the South region being the lowest (as found in the contingency tables section), the average price per product sold is the highest in the Southern region. However, the highest median price per product is highest in the West. This implies that the South buys more high-ticket items to drag up the mean, while the smaller-ticket items sold in the West generally cost more.

Quantities kept on hand are fairly static across our regions.

As for discounts, the average is highest in the Central Region and Lowest in the West region, with the median being lower than the mean for all regions, implying that most items are not on sale, but there is the occasional "big sale". 

Mean and median profit is highest in the West, and lowest in the Central Region, with the difference between mean and median being similar to the general statistics.


### Segment Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Segment) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```

Despite Home Office having the lowest number of products sold, it has the highest average price per item, though the lowest median price. This implies that Home Office purchasers buy the highest ticket items, but mostly lower ticket items in terms of quantity.

### Category Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```

Office supplies were found to be the most frequent purchase, but unsurprisingly they have the lowest mean and median sales price. 
Technology, which was the least frequent purchase, has the highest average price, while furniture has the highest median. This implies the tech has the highest ticket items, but also a large number of lower ticket items, while furniture items generally cost more, but don't usually reach the high ticket cost of the most expensive tech items.

### Region and Segment Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Region, Segment) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```

The highest average product price was for Home Offices in the South, while the highest median product price was for Corporate purchases in the East. The lowest average product price was for Consumers in the Central Region,  while the lowest median product price was for Corporate purchases in the Central Region.


### Segment and Category Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Segment, Category) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```

The highest mean and median sales are Home Office Technology purchases. The lowest mean sales are Home Office Office Supplies, and the lowest median sales are Consumer Office Supplies. 

### Category and Region Numerical Summaries

```{r}
store_df |>
  group_by(Category, Region) |>
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), 
                   list("mean" = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), "median" = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                   .names = "{.fn}_{.col}"))
```


The highest mean product price is Technology purchases in the east, and the highest median product price is furniture purchases in the west. The lowest mean product price is Office Supplies in the West, and the lowest median product price is Office Supplies in the Central Region.

# Graphical Summaries

## Bar Charts 

### Frequency Bar Charts

First, I will make bar charts for sales frequency based on Region, Segment, and Category.

```{r}
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Region,fill=Region))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(y="Frequency",title="Frequency of Product Purchases by Region")+
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Category,fill=Category))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(y="Frequency",title="Frequency of Product Purchases by Category")+
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Segment,fill=Segment))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(y="Frequency",title="Frequency of Product Purchases by Segment")+
  theme_minimal()
```

### Sales Bar Charts

Next, I will make bar charts for total sales based on Region, Segment, and Category.

```{r}
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Region,y=Sales,fill=Region))+
  geom_col()+
  labs(title="Total Sales by Region")+
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Category,y=Sales,fill=Category))+
  geom_col()+
  labs(title="Total Sales by Category")+
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(data=store_df,aes(x=Segment,y=Sales,fill=Segment))+
  geom_col()+
  labs(title="Total Sales by Segment")+
  theme_minimal()
```
## Side-by-Side Bar Charts

Moving on from simple bar charts, we will make Side-by-Side Bar Charts for Sales based on combinations of our categorical variables.

```{r}
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Region, y=Sales, x=Segment)) + 
    geom_bar(position="dodge", stat="identity")
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Region, y=Sales, x=Category)) + 
    geom_bar(position="dodge", stat="identity")
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Category, y=Sales, x=Segment)) + 
    geom_bar(position="dodge", stat="identity")
```

## Histograms

Next up, I will create histograms to view the distribution of product prices and profit per item. For these histograms, we run into a scaling problem, where the histogram is essentially illegible if all values are visible. 

Thus, I adjusted the domain and range of of the graphs, as the out of bounds values were so small they weren't visible anyway, at least not without making the bins so large that the graph becomes useless.

I also chose to add faceting to the second plot, as we haven't previously explored the interaction between profit and our categorical variables.

```{r}
ggplot(store_df, aes(x = Sales)) + 
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, fill = "blue")+
  xlim(0, 6000) +
  ylim(0, 2000) +
  labs(x = "Product Price",y = "Frequency",title = "Frequency of Product Prices")
ggplot(store_df, aes(x = Profit)) + 
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 100, fill = "blue")+
  xlim(-800, 800) +
  ylim(0, 8000) +
  labs(x = "Profit Amount",y = "Frequency",title = "Frequency of Profit Amounts")+
  facet_wrap(vars(Region))
```
## Box Plots

For the sake of trying pretty much every graph type, here's a grouped box plot. For this particular dataset, these plots aren't particularly appealing to look at, but it is kind of interesting.

```{r}
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Region, y=Sales, x=Segment)) + 
    geom_boxplot()
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Region, y=Sales, x=Category)) + 
    geom_boxplot()
ggplot(store_df, aes(fill=Category, y=Sales, x=Segment)) + 
    geom_boxplot()
```

## Scatter Plot

Now this is a fascinating scatter plot. Obviously, you'd expect a fairly standard linear relationship, and while that's sort of true, you can also see the effect of discount/clearance sales for below profitability. 

```{r}
ggplot(store_df, aes(x=Sales,y=Profit,color=Region)) + 
    geom_point()
```
